newsitem.title: UK: EU Green rules drive gas oil prices higher.
newsitem.headline: EU Green rules drive gas oil prices higher.

text.p: Green rules for European diesel fuel have helped push gas oil prices to their highest level since the Gulf War in 1991.

Although mounting tension in oil-rich Iraq pushed the price of front month gas oil futures on the International Petroleum Exchange as high as $206 a tonne on Monday, the new regulations have boosted the new cleaner-burning diesel $15 above that.
From October 1, all European Union countries must sell the new diesel with a maximum sulphur content of 0.05 percent, compared to the current limit of 0.20 percent.
Traders are divided on whether the impact of the lower sulphur content has been overstated.

"It's difficult to see the wood from the trees. Half the people I speak to think supply is balanced to slightly short; the other half I speak to think we're balanced to slightly long," one trader said.
Few traders see any great shortage of 0.05 percent material, but many believe there could be some higher premiums when the regulations first come into force.
"There's bound to be some market hype with the changeover, which could send premiums higher initially," one trader said.
"The major refineries have the equipment in place to produce low sulphur. There may be a few hiccups but these will soon be ironed out," a trader at a U.K.-based refinery said.

It costs roughly $6 to $8 a tonne more to produce 0.05 percent than 0.2 percent, but low sulphur is currently trading at a $10 per tonne premium over 0.2 percent material. Swaps traders see low sulphur trading $10.50 over 0.2 percent for the fourth quarter.

But some physical traders are more bullish, and a number of key suppliers are reported to be stockpiling 0.05 percent material on the expectation that premiums will shoot up immediately before and for two to three months after October 1.
"We've got some spare storage which we may put to use. It looks like it might be worth holding onto low sulphur for the time being," one trader said.

Market players said one German trading house had been snapping up low sulphur material since the spring and putting it into storage in Rotterdam. A French refiner was also reported to be buying heavily.

In the Mediterranean, major Italian refiners said they were on target to satisfy their commitments, although some North European traders question this. Algeria has also guaranteed 0.05 spec material but at a price. As in northern Europe, refiners are expecting hefty premiums.
"We'll be looking for a premium of $12 to $13 over 0.2 percent for low sulphur material for the rest of the year," a spokesman at a major Italian refinery said.
"These premiums reflect not just the extra cost of producing the low sulphur material but also the logistical costs of segregating storage," he added.
